takeaways.q: What is the PRIMARY mechanism Claude uses for tool selection?
takeaways.a: Tool descriptions — not supplementary metadata or an afterthought.

takeaways.q: Five elements of a production-grade tool description?
takeaways.a: Purpose; expected inputs with types and constraints; example queries; edge cases and limitations; explicit boundaries versus similar tools.

takeaways.q: When is expanding tool descriptions the right fix for misrouting — and when not?
takeaways.a: Right when the agent has a workable number of tools but can't tell them apart. Not when the toolkit itself is overloaded (beyond ~4–5 tools per agent).

takeaways.q: Why are few-shot examples a poor FIRST step for tool misrouting?
takeaways.a: They add token overhead without fixing the root cause — weak descriptions. Fix descriptions first.

takeaways.q: When several remedies would work, which does the exam favour?
takeaways.a: Low-effort, high-leverage fixes: better descriptions before routing classifiers, scoped access before full access, community servers before custom builds.

takeaways.q: How should a vague generic tool be improved?
takeaways.a: Split it into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts and narrow, clearly described jobs.

takeaways.q: What can silently override well-written tool descriptions?
takeaways.a: Keyword-sensitive instructions in the system prompt that create unintended tool associations — review the system prompt after updating descriptions.

traps.trap: Choosing few-shot examples to fix tool misrouting caused by minimal descriptions
traps.why: Few-shot adds token overhead without fixing the root cause. The model is confused because descriptions don't differentiate the tools — fix descriptions first.

traps.trap: Implementing a routing classifier as the first step to fix tool selection
traps.why: Over-engineered as a first response; bypasses the LLM's language understanding and adds infrastructure the exam doesn't consider proportionate.

traps.trap: Consolidating similar tools into one as the first step
traps.why: Consolidation is a valid long-term choice but costs more than expanding descriptions. The exam favours low-effort, high-leverage first steps.

traps.trap: Ignoring system prompt wording after updating tool descriptions
traps.why: Keyword-sensitive system prompt instructions can silently override good descriptions and create unintended tool associations.

takeaways.q: What is the isError flag for in MCP tool responses?
takeaways.a: It tells the model the tool execution failed, so it reasons about recovery instead of treating error text as a successful result.

takeaways.q: Protocol errors vs tool execution errors?
takeaways.a: Protocol errors: JSON-RPC errors for malformed requests (unknown tool, invalid schema). Execution errors: result objects with isError: true — the tool ran but failed.

takeaways.q: Four error categories and their recovery?
takeaways.a: Transient → retry after delay. Validation → fix input and resend. Business → escalate / alternative workflow. Permission → different credentials or escalate.

takeaways.q: When is isRetryable true?
takeaways.a: Only for transient errors (valid request, system temporarily unavailable). All other categories are false — something must change first.

takeaways.q: Distinction the exam tests most directly here?
takeaways.a: Access failure (couldn't reach the data source → isError: true) vs valid empty result (query succeeded, no matches → isError: false).

takeaways.q: Why does confusing access failures with empty results break recovery?
takeaways.a: The agent retries a successful query that legitimately found nothing — wasted effort, possibly wrong escalation.

takeaways.q: Three metadata fields of a structured error?
takeaways.a: errorCategory (transient/validation/business/permission), isRetryable (boolean), description (explanation + recovery guidance).

takeaways.q: Error-handling principle for subagents?
takeaways.a: Recover locally from transient failures; propagate only what can't be resolved locally — with partial results and what was attempted.

traps.trap: Retrying when a tool returns an empty result from a successful query
traps.why: Empty from a successful query means no data matches. Retrying returns the same. Accept the result and respond accordingly.

traps.trap: Using generic error messages like 'Operation failed' without structured metadata
traps.why: Without errorCategory, isRetryable and description, the agent can't tell transient failures from business-rule violations.

traps.trap: Treating business errors as retryable
traps.why: A policy violation (e.g., refund over limit) never resolves on retry. Take an alternative path such as escalation.

traps.trap: Marking a validation error isRetryable: true because the agent can recover from it
traps.why: isRetryable asks whether resending THIS EXACT call can work. A malformed ID fails every time (false). The agent recovers by correcting input; errorCategory carries that instruction.

traps.trap: Reading isRetryable: false as 'abandon the task'
traps.why: Three categories are non-retryable but only two are dead ends. Validation = fix input; business and permission = alternative path or different principal.

traps.trap: Silently suppressing subagent errors by returning empty results as success
traps.why: Hides failure from the coordinator — it can't distinguish 'found nothing' from 'could not search' and may produce incomplete output.

takeaways.q: Optimal number of tools per agent?
takeaways.a: About 4–5, scoped to the agent's role. More tools degrade selection reliability.

takeaways.q: When do you consolidate tools into one parameterised tool?
takeaways.a: When they're variations on one job with the same shape (data in, operation, data out).

takeaways.q: Decision rule: sharpen descriptions vs split by role vs consolidate?
takeaways.a: Few confusing tools → sharpen descriptions. Different jobs → split by role (4–5 each). Variations on one job → consolidate into a parameterised tool.

takeaways.q: tool_choice: "auto"?
takeaways.a: Model decides whether to call a tool or reply with text. Default for general operation.

takeaways.q: tool_choice: "any"?
takeaways.a: Model MUST call a tool but picks which. Guarantees structured output from one of several schemas rather than plain text.

takeaways.q: Forced tool_choice ({type: "tool", name})?
takeaways.a: Model MUST call that specific tool. Enforces a mandatory workflow step — can't be skipped or reordered.

takeaways.q: What is a scoped cross-role tool?
takeaways.a: A constrained version of another role's capability given directly to an agent (e.g., verify_fact on the synthesis agent) to avoid coordinator round-trips for high-frequency simple operations.

takeaways.q: How does least privilege apply to tools?
takeaways.a: Replace generic tools with constrained ones that do exactly what the agent needs (load_document instead of fetch_url).

traps.trap: Routing all simple verification requests through the coordinator when 85% are simple lookups
traps.why: Each round-trip adds hops. A scoped verify_fact tool on the synthesis agent handles the simple 85% directly and cuts latency substantially.

traps.trap: Using tool_choice 'auto' when structured output is required
traps.why: With auto the model may reply in text. Use 'any' to guarantee a tool call, or forced selection for a specific tool.

traps.trap: Giving an agent 18 tools and expecting reliable selection
traps.why: Selection reliability drops as tool count rises. Aim for 4–5 per agent.

traps.trap: Giving a subagent a generic fetch_url tool when a constrained load_document would suffice
traps.why: Generic tools enable misuse. Constrained alternatives enforce least privilege and make purpose clearer.

takeaways.q: Where does team-wide MCP server config live?
takeaways.a: .mcp.json at the project root — version-controlled and shared with everyone who clones the repo.

takeaways.q: What is ~/.claude.json for (MCP)?
takeaways.a: User-level: personal, experimental or test servers. Not version-controlled, not shared.

takeaways.q: How do you keep credentials out of .mcp.json?
takeaways.a: Environment variable expansion: ${GITHUB_TOKEN}. Each developer sets it locally; secrets never enter history.

takeaways.q: What does ${VAR:-default} do?
takeaways.a: Expands to VAR when set, falls back to default when unset — good for machine-specific paths.

takeaways.q: MCP resources vs tools — what do resources add?
takeaways.a: Resources expose content catalogues (schemas, docs, summaries) upfront, cutting wasted exploratory tool calls. Tools perform actions.

takeaways.q: Community vs custom MCP server?
takeaways.a: Community for standard integrations (Jira, GitHub, Slack). Custom only for team-specific workflows community servers can't handle.

takeaways.q: Why do sparse MCP tool descriptions cause problems?
takeaways.a: The agent prefers built-in tools with rich descriptions. Enhance MCP descriptions to explain capabilities and outputs.

takeaways.q: How are MCP tools discovered?
takeaways.a: Tools from all configured servers (project and user level) are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously.

traps.trap: Building a custom MCP server for a standard integration like Jira
traps.why: Evaluate community servers first. Custom builds are justified only for team-specific workflows.

traps.trap: Putting team-wide MCP server configuration in ~/.claude.json
traps.why: ~/.claude.json is personal and unshared. Team-wide servers belong in .mcp.json at the project root.

traps.trap: Committing credentials directly in .mcp.json instead of using environment variable expansion
traps.why: Credentials in version control are a security risk. Use ${GITHUB_TOKEN} so each dev sets tokens locally.

traps.trap: Leaving MCP tool descriptions sparse, causing the agent to prefer built-in tools
traps.why: The model defaults to tools it understands best. Enhance MCP descriptions to compete for selection.

takeaways.q: Grep vs Glob?
takeaways.a: Grep searches file CONTENTS (function calls, error messages, imports). Glob matches file PATHS/NAMES (**/*.test.tsx, config files).

takeaways.q: Tool sequence to find callers of a deprecated function and their tests?
takeaways.a: Grep the function name → callers; Glob for sibling test files by naming convention; Grep again for wrapper names to catch indirect usage.

takeaways.q: Correct approach to modifying a file?
takeaways.a: Edit first with a short unique anchor. On non-unique match, Read + Write is the exam's documented fallback (real Claude Code also offers widening old_string / replace_all).

takeaways.q: Incremental codebase understanding strategy?
takeaways.a: Grep for entry points → Read to trace flows and imports → Grep for wrapper/exported names → Read only justified files. Never load everything upfront.

takeaways.q: Why does Edit fail on non-unique text?
takeaways.a: Unique matching is a safety mechanism against changing unintended occurrences.

takeaways.q: How do you trace usage through wrappers and barrel files?
takeaways.a: Grep for the definition, Read the defining file to find exported names, then Grep each exported name across the codebase.

takeaways.q: Exam answer when Edit reports a non-unique anchor?
takeaways.a: Read the full file, then Write the complete modified version — the exam guide's keyed fallback.

traps.trap: Using Glob to find function callers (it searches paths, not contents)
traps.why: Glob matches file paths. Use Grep to search inside files for function names, imports, or error messages.

traps.trap: Using Grep to find files by extension or naming pattern
traps.why: Glob is the purpose-built path matcher: **/*.test.tsx, **/config.*.

traps.trap: Reading all source files upfront before understanding what is relevant
traps.why: Context-budget killer. Go incremental: Grep for entry points, then Read specific flows.

traps.trap: Defaulting to Read + Write for every file modification instead of trying Edit first
traps.why: Edit touches only the specific text and uses less context. Read + Write is the fallback when Edit can't find a unique anchor.

traps.trap: Answering 'widen old_string or set replace_all' when a question asks what to do after Edit reports a non-unique match
traps.why: That's current Claude Code behaviour, but the exam guide names Read + Write as the fallback and keyed answers follow the guide.
